🗃️ Building a Personal Feature Store
description:
A feature store (like Feast) solves training/serving skew by defining a feature once and serving it consistently to both batch training jobs and low-latency online inference.

- Offline store: historical feature values for training (usually a data warehouse table)
- Online store: latest feature values, low-latency lookup (usually a key-value store)
- The feature definition is shared between both, preventing subtle train/serve mismatches
- Overkill for a single model; valuable once you have more than one consumer of the same features

title: 📡 Kafka/Redpanda Streaming Ingestion for Vector Pipelines
description:
Weeks 04-05 built the index and the ranking function; neither gets fed by itself. Something has to notice a claim was filed, updated, or reopened, turn it into an embedding, and land it in the vector store continuously, not as a nightly batch.

- Partition assignment and keying strategy determine ordering guarantees and skew -- get this wrong and events for the same claim can process out of order
- Idempotent upsert (content-hash keyed) is what makes at-least-once delivery safe to replay without duplicating or corrupting index state
- Micro-batching with bounded concurrency and backoff is how a consumer keeps up without overwhelming the embedding API or vector store
- A dead-letter queue with a real replay plan is not optional -- malformed events will happen, and silently dropping them is a data-integrity failure

title: ⌚ Reverse-Engineering Fitness & Health Algorithms
description:
WHOOP and Oura's proprietary Strain/Readiness scores are built from the same raw signals your Garmin already exposes: HRV, resting heart rate, and sleep stages. Understanding their published methodology lets you approximate the same insight on your own data.

- HRV (heart rate variability) trend, not absolute value, is what predicts recovery
- Sleep-stage proportions (deep/REM/light) matter more than total sleep duration alone
- Strain-style scores combine heart-rate-zone time under a load curve, not just step count
- Garmin's raw FIT files expose all the same underlying signals WHOOP/Oura compute their scores from

title: 🏚️ Streaming Vector Infra Against Legacy Sources
description:
Week 06 built the pipeline: Kafka topics, consumer groups, idempotent upsert into the vector index. This topic's lesson is that the source sets the latency floor -- no amount of downstream engineering makes a mainframe nightly batch extract into real-time data, a real and common constraint in BFSI where core systems are still on-prem MSSQL/Oracle or COBOL mainframes with only partial cloud migration.

- Change data capture (CDC) on MSSQL/Oracle has real mechanics -- sys.sp_cdc_enable_table, DBMS_LOGMNR -- with real latency and load implications
- A watermark/staleness contract is how downstream consumers know how fresh (or stale) the data behind a retrieval result actually is
- Event-time vs. processing-time merging matters when a legacy batch extract lands hours after the events it describes
- Being honest about your source's real latency floor is a design input, not a failure to engineer around

title: 🕵️ Stealing Modern Web Scraper Anti-Detection
description:
Commercial scraping networks survive at scale by mimicking real browser fingerprints at every layer -- TLS handshake, HTTP headers, and JS-detectable automation flags -- not just rotating IPs.

- TLS/JA3 fingerprinting can identify a non-browser HTTP client even through a real proxy
- Headless browsers leak automation flags (navigator.webdriver) unless explicitly patched
- Residential proxy rotation defeats IP-based rate limiting, not fingerprint-based detection
- Ethical/ToS note: this is defensive knowledge for understanding detection, not a license to violate a site's terms

title: 🎮 Reverse-Engineering Duolingo's Gamification Loop
description:
Duolingo's engagement loop combines spaced repetition (reviewing material right before you'd forget it) with streak/loss-aversion mechanics. Both are copyable patterns for any personal learning app.

- Spaced repetition schedules review intervals based on how well you answered last time, not a fixed calendar
- Streaks exploit loss aversion -- losing a 30-day streak feels worse than never having one
- Difficulty adapts per-user: too easy loses engagement, too hard causes drop-off
- The core loop (learn -> quiz -> spaced review) is a small state machine, not a complex ML system

title: ✂️ Semantic Chunking Strategies
description:
Week 08 turned a scanned form or PDF into clean text and structured elements. Before any of that text can be embedded and searched, it has to be split into pieces small enough for an embedding model's context window and a retrieval system's relevance granularity -- and splitting badly silently degrades every downstream retrieval result.

- Fixed-size chunking is the simplest baseline but routinely cuts sentences and arguments in half
- Semantic chunking (splitting on meaning boundaries, not just character counts) generally retrieves better but costs more to compute
- Chunk size is a real tuning parameter that trades off retrieval precision against context completeness -- there's no universal right size
- Overlap between chunks is a deliberate mitigation for boundary information loss, not free insurance

title: 🎓 Copying Khan Academy's Socratic AI Tutor
description:
Khanmigo's tutoring persona is enforced through prompting and a state machine that tracks what's already been revealed, so the AI nudges toward understanding instead of just stating the answer.

- System prompt explicitly forbids stating the final answer directly, only guiding questions
- A state machine tracks how many hints have been given, escalating specificity gradually
- The tutor deliberately asks the student to explain their reasoning before validating it
- This pattern generalizes beyond math -- any 'teach, don't tell' assistant needs the same guardrails

title: 🧪 Synthetic Data Curation for FinServ
description:
This topic is about what feeds a dev/test environment before any real data does. In a regulated industry, testing a new pipeline against real claims or policy data carries real compliance risk -- realistic synthetic data lets engineering move fast without that exposure.

- Realistic synthetic data needs correct statistical distributions, not just plausible-looking individual records
- Referential integrity across synthetic tables (a synthetic claim referencing a synthetic policy) has to be maintained deliberately
- Domain-specific generators (policy numbers, claim statuses, realistic date sequences) beat generic fake-data libraries for BFSI-specific fields
- Synthetic data is a compliance control, not just a testing convenience -- it removes real-PII exposure from non-production environments entirely

title: 🔄 Incremental Embedding Updates
description:
Weeks 01-07 built the index; this topic keeps it honest after that. A vector index is not a write-once artifact -- the documents behind it keep changing, and the embedding model behind it eventually changes too. Neither event is optional to handle.

- Content-hash-based change detection is what tells you a document actually changed, not just that it was touched
- Re-embedding on every model upgrade is expensive at scale -- a staleness/freshness gate lets you decide what's worth re-embedding now vs. later
- Idempotent upsert (from Week 06's pattern) is what makes incremental updates safe to retry without corrupting the index
- An embedding-model version is itself metadata worth tracking per vector, not an implicit assumption

title: 📊 Reverse-Engineering Bloomberg Terminal Analytics
description:
Bloomberg-style analytics start from the same raw material anyone has -- transactions -- and impose a consistent categorization and normalization layer to produce dynamic cash-flow and balance-sheet views.

- The hard part isn't the math, it's consistent categorization of messy, inconsistently-labeled transactions
- A dynamic cash-flow model recomputes forward projections whenever new transactions arrive
- Balance sheets need point-in-time snapshots, not just a running transaction log
- Most personal finance dashboards skip reconciliation -- verifying computed balances against actual account balances

title: 🕸️ DataPrep Pipeline Orchestration
description:
The previous topics each built one stage of a real DataPrep pipeline in isolation: parse a document, chunk it, decide when to re-embed it. This topic wires those stages together into one orchestrated pipeline and treats the orchestration itself as a first-class engineering problem, not just glue code.

- DAG-based orchestration (the same pattern behind Airflow) makes a multi-stage pipeline's dependencies and retry behavior explicit
- Idempotent task design (deterministic IDs, safe-to-retry writes) is what makes a pipeline recoverable after a partial failure, not just after a clean run
- Each stage (parse, chunk, embed, upsert) should be independently retryable without re-running the whole pipeline from scratch
- Orchestration failures need visibility -- a silently-stuck pipeline stage is worse than one that fails loudly

title: 📉 Copying Quantitative Finance Risk Signals
description:
Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Monte Carlo simulation are the standard tools quant desks use to answer 'how much could I realistically lose?' -- both are directly applicable to a personal investment portfolio.

- VaR answers: 'with 95% confidence, I won't lose more than $X over the next N days'
- Monte Carlo simulation runs thousands of random future price paths to estimate a full outcome distribution, not just one number
- Historical VaR uses actual past returns; parametric VaR assumes a normal distribution (often wrong for real markets)
- The value isn't a precise number -- it's building the habit of thinking in distributions, not point estimates

title: 🖥️ DataPrep for COBOL/Mainframe-Sourced Documents
description:
Real BFSI DataPrep can't assume its input source is a reasonably modern document. A large share of core transaction and policy data in Israeli (and much real-world) FinServ still lives on COBOL mainframes -- this topic is about extracting usable data from that world into a modern pipeline.

- Copybooks define fixed-width record layouts via byte offsets -- there's no self-describing schema, you parse against the copybook definition
- EBCDIC is a different character encoding than ASCII/UTF-8 -- reading mainframe extracts wrong here produces silently garbled text, not an error
- COMP-3 (packed decimal) and zoned-decimal formats pack numeric data at the byte level -- getting the unpacking wrong corrupts numbers silently
- This is a real, common BFSI constraint, not a legacy edge case -- partial cloud migration is the norm, not the exception, in this industry

title: 📄 Stealing Modern ATS Resume Parsers
description:
Applicant Tracking Systems parse resumes into structured fields and score them against a job description's keywords and requirements -- understanding this scoring logic lets a personal job-search agent optimize against it directly.

- ATS parsing often breaks on complex formatting (tables, columns, graphics) -- plain structured text parses most reliably
- Keyword matching against the job description is still the dominant signal in most ATS scoring
- Section headers matter: ATS systems look for standard headers (Experience, Education, Skills) to parse correctly
- A resume that reads well to a human can still score poorly if it doesn't parse cleanly to a machine first
